title: Rabies Deaths Spike: Vietnam's Unregulated Dog Trade Becomes Public Health Crisis
excerpt: Seven rabies deaths in Tây Ninh province in early 2026—all preventable. Vietnam's unregulated dog meat supply chain is amplifying disease transmission and overwhelming local health systems, even as 95% of Vietnamese want the trade to end.
body_html:
The Bottom Line

In the first four months of 2026, Tây Ninh province recorded seven rabies deaths—all from unvaccinated individuals bitten by infected dogs. Vietnam's completely unregulated dog meat supply chain is creating a perfect storm for disease transmission: dogs moved without health checks, slaughter sites with zero sanitation oversight, and a public health system struggling to keep pace. The irony is stark: 95% of Vietnamese support ending the trade, yet the infrastructure to regulate it safely barely exists.

Key Findings

Rabies Deaths Double as Vaccination Coverage Remains Below 35%

Tây Ninh province's seven rabies fatalities in early 2026 represent a public health emergency that stretches beyond individual tragedy. All victims had direct contact with infected dogs and none received post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) vaccination in time. Critically, the province's dog vaccination rate stands at just 34.4% across its 192,700–198,000 canine population—far below the WHO-recommended 70% threshold for herd protection. In an unregulated trade where dogs are transported alive across provinces without health documentation, infected animals can spread rabies across provincial borders before symptoms manifest.

The connection is direct: Đắk Lắk province, where the dog meat trade is economically significant, recorded 27 rabies deaths between 2019–2024, with 7 cases in both 2024 and 2025—the highest rate in Vietnam. The pattern is consistent: loose dog management, high free-roaming populations, and the absence of mandatory health screening in the meat supply chain create ideal conditions for disease spillover.

Zero Registered Slaughterhouses: Food Safety in the Shadows

In Hanoi's Tây Mỗ Ward alone, authorities identified three illegal dog and cat slaughter sites operating on Hữu Hưng Street in early 2026, issuing administrative violations for all three. These are not licensed facilities—there are no registered dog slaughterhouses in Vietnam. This legal vacuum means zero temperature monitoring, no microbial testing for E. coli or Salmonella, and no traceability. When two men in Tân Kỳ, Nghệ An suffered severe burns (38% body surface area) on April 28, 2026, while using propane to scald dog carcasses, the incident exposed not just occupational hazard but the broader reality: no safety standards, no worker protections, no food safety oversight.

Unregulated slaughter creates conditions where zoonotic pathogens thrive. Without mandatory health screening of source animals, rabies, E. coli, and other foodborne pathogens move directly from unvaccinated dogs into the supply chain and onto tables.

95% of Vietnamese Want Change—But Government Structures Lag Behind Public Will

Here is the critical disconnect: while 95% of Vietnamese surveyed in 2021 support ending the dog meat trade, the government's regulatory response remains rooted in *managing* the trade rather than phasing it out. Hanoi's directives in early 2026 focus on inspecting slaughter sites and mandating closures by June 30, 2026—but these are local enforcement measures, not national legislation. In contrast, Bali, Indonesia criminalized the dog meat trade in 2025 after a seven-year advocacy campaign. Vietnam has no equivalent national ban.

The public health implication is profound: without a clear legal phase-out, supply chains remain fragmented and uncontrollable. Disease surveillance becomes impossible. Health systems in rural provinces like Tây Ninh and Đắk Lắk continue absorbing rabies cases that are entirely preventable through regulated animal health standards or trade elimination.

Nationwide Rabies Burden: 82–84 Deaths Annually, Driven by Trade-Related Animal Movement

Vietnam recorded 82 rabies deaths nationally in 2023 and 84 in 2024. While not all are linked to the dog meat trade, the trade amplifies the problem: dogs are transported alive across provinces, often confined in crowded cages without health documentation. An infected dog in a shipment destined for slaughter becomes a mobile disease vector. Rural and mountainous areas—where the trade is economically entrenched and health system capacity is weakest—bear the highest burden. The WHO recommends dog vaccination reaching ≥80% of the canine population to prevent spillover; Vietnam's average is far below.

Also Worth Noting

  • Pet theft networks surge alongside unregulated slaughter operations — Hanoi police in late April 2026 dismantled organized dog and cat theft rings, exposing the supply chain's reliance on stolen animals that bypass any health screening.
  • Hanoi's 3-clade slaughter site crackdown reveals scale of illegal operations — Administrative fines totaling 21 million VND were issued in Tây Mỗ Ward for unlicensed slaughter, yet the sites continue operating because no alternative livelihoods exist for traders.
  • Bali's criminalization model offers a tested playbook — After seven years of advocacy, Indonesia's Bali province criminalized dog meat trade in 2025, providing lessons for Vietnam's transition toward a full national ban with worker retraining and livelihood support.
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis education remains critically underfunded in high-risk provinces — Most rabies deaths in Tây Ninh and Đắk Lắk involve delayed or absent PEP vaccination; rural communities lack awareness and access to emergency medical response.
  • Tây Ninh province declared a diphtheria outbreak in April 2026 requiring mandatory dog vaccination drives — The province is now mandating 15-minute wound washing with soap, immediate PEP vaccination, and expanded canine vaccination campaigns—reactive measures that could be prevented through trade regulation.

Take Action: Sign the petition to support Vietnam's roadmap toward eliminating the dog meat trade by 2030 and strengthening public health protections for all communities.

Every rabies death in Vietnam is preventable. In the first four months of 2026, Tây Ninh province lost seven people to rabies—all of them unvaccinated after contact with infected dogs. Not one of these deaths needed to happen.

Vietnam's dog meat trade operates in complete legal darkness. Zero registered slaughterhouses. Zero health screening. Zero food safety oversight. Dogs are transported alive across provinces without vaccination records or disease testing. When they reach illegal slaughter sites, there's no temperature monitoring, no microbial testing, no accountability. An infected dog becomes a disease vector that affects entire communities.

The hardest part? **95% of Vietnamese support ending this trade.** But while public opinion is overwhelming, government structures still focus on *managing* the trade rather than phasing it out. Meanwhile, rabies continues spreading, health systems in rural provinces are overwhelmed, and workers suffer in unsafe conditions—like the two men who were severely burned in Tân Kỳ in April while processing dog meat with propane.

Vietnam doesn't need to accept this. Bali criminalized the dog meat trade in 2025. We can do this too—with worker transition support, clear timelines, and a commitment to the 95% of Vietnamese who are ready for change.
